title: Family Needs
intro: Standard supply lists are written for healthy adults. This module covers what babies, children, people who rely on medicines or equipment, older relatives and pets need on top of them. Medication lists and care instructions stay on paper with you.

actions.title: Make a feeding plan for your baby
actions.why: A baby cannot wait or change foods, and formula made with unsafe water or fed from unclean bottles can make a baby seriously ill.
actions.how: If you breastfeed, keep going: CDC calls it the safest way to feed a baby in an emergency. If your baby has formula, stock the formula your baby already takes. Where it is sold ready-to-feed, stock that form, because it needs no water or mixing, with one sealed bottle for each feed. Where it is sold only as powder, stock unopened powder and sealed bottled water measured for every feed, plus water for washing bottles (U3-08), and mix each feed fresh. Count it in feeds, not fluid ounces: feeds a day multiplied by your target days. The site's number uses 8 feeds a day and labels that as an assumption; babies take fewer feeds as they grow, and the American Academy of Pediatrics says 4 or 5 a day by 6 months. Count your own baby's feeds on a normal day and change the figure in your household setup. Add disposable cups, a new one for each feed, for when bottles and nipples cannot be washed in safe water. Mix powder with bottled water until officials say the tap water is safe. Use prepared formula within 2 hours of preparing it and within 1 hour of the start of a feed, then throw away what is left.
actions.done: Your household setup shows your own baby's feeds a day, and for a formula-fed baby the formula for each feed (ready-to-feed, or powder with sealed bottled water) and a disposable cup for each feed are stored together.

actions.title: Stock diapers and wipes for your target days
actions.why: Stores may be closed or empty in the first days, and diapers are among the first things to sell out.
actions.how: The site works out how many diapers you need from your household setup, at 8 a day for each child in diapers, which is this site's assumption; a newborn uses more, so check the number against what you really use on a normal day. Buy it in your child's current size plus one pack of the next size up, with wipes, diaper cream and small bags for used diapers. Use from this stock and replace it as you go, so the sizes keep up with your child.
actions.done: The number of diapers the site works out is stored in your child's current size, with one pack of the next size, wipes, diaper cream and small bags.

actions.title: Carry your baby or small child down the stairs in a carrier, not a stroller
actions.why: With the elevators out, a carrier leaves both hands free for the handrail, and a stroller on the stairs blocks everyone behind you.
actions.how: Get a soft carrier or sling rated for your child's weight and fit it the way the maker's instructions show for your child's age. A child aged 1 to 3 rides on your back in a carrier rated for their weight. With a child on your back, wear your bag on your front, or have the second adult or the named helper (FN-33) carry it. Practice once: put the child in, pick up your bag, and walk down your stairwell holding the rail; practice the back carry once on your own stairs too. Keep the carrier with your bag by the door, and leave the stroller behind in an evacuation unless your way out is step-free from door to street.
actions.done: You have walked down your stairwell with your child in the carrier, your bag on your front or carried by another adult, and a hand on the rail, and the carrier is kept with your bag.
actions.cite_todo: Official source on leaving a building with an infant in a carrier and on safe carrier positioning (AAP HealthyChildren or CPSC).

actions.title: Keep each child's medicines and a dosing syringe together
actions.why: A child's dose depends on weight, and guessing it in the dark with a kitchen spoon is how mistakes happen.
actions.how: Ask your pediatrician or pharmacist now which fever and pain medicine suits each child's age, and the dose for their current weight. Write the answer by hand on the printable medication list, and update it as the child grows. Keep an unopened bottle of that medicine, the oral syringe that comes with it, marked in milliliters, a digital thermometer, any prescribed medicines and, for a baby, diaper cream in one bag. Do not give acetaminophen to a child under 2 years unless a doctor has told you to and given you the dose for their weight. A baby under 12 weeks with a fever, a rectal temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher, is seen by a doctor before any medicine: call your pediatrician's 24-hour line or go to an emergency department. If more than one adult gives a child medicine, keep one dose sheet with the medicine, write on it the time, the medicine, the amount and who gave it, and read it before every dose; this is this site's suggestion.
actions.done: Each child's fever medicine, the oral syringe that came with it, the dose for their current weight and a dose sheet are packed together.

actions.title: Plan how to keep your baby cool or warm without power
actions.why: Babies overheat and lose heat faster than adults and cannot tell you which is happening.
actions.how: Put a thermometer in the room where the baby sleeps; sustained indoor heat above about 88 °F (31 °C) is dangerous for babies. In heat, use your coolest room, dress the baby in one light layer, offer feeds more often and wipe their skin with a cool damp cloth. Do not wait for a number: move a baby somewhere cooler as soon as you cannot keep them comfortable and feeding normally. In cold, dress the baby in one more layer than you are wearing, or in a wearable blanket, and warm them against your body while you are awake. A hat is for when the baby is awake and held, never for sleep. For sleep the baby goes on their back on a firm, flat surface of their own, such as a crib, bassinet or portable play yard set up beside you in the warm room, with no loose blankets, pillows or soft toys: not in an adult bed or sleeping bag, on a couch, in a car seat or inside the blanket shelter with others. If you cannot keep the room warm enough for the baby dressed this way, leave for a warm place (HC-21) without waiting.
actions.done: A thermometer is in the room where your baby sleeps, and every adult at home can point to the coolest room and the warm room you would use.
actions.cite_todo: A CDC or AAP source for offering feeds more often in heat; CDC's page on infants and heat says only to make sure they drink plenty of fluids.

actions.title: Test-carry your real load down your stairs
actions.why: The bag weights on this site are for an adult carrying only a bag, and with a child on your back or front the real load can be double.
actions.how: Test the worst ordinary case: one adult at home alone with every child and pet who could be there. Put each child who cannot walk a mile into their carrier, and put on your packed bag: on your front if a child rides on your back, or handed to the second adult or the named helper. Walk down your stairs and once around the block, keeping one hand free for the rail. If one adult would be carrying two children, or the load is more than you can manage, change the plan now: move food, water and spare clothes to the other adult's bag, the car kit or the place you would go, and name a neighbor who has agreed to carry one child or one bag (FN-33). With a second adult, a light folded stroller can be carried down for the walk on the street. If it still does not work, plan to leave earlier (X2-05); do not solve it by leaving out the child's own supplies or by counting on a toddler to walk the whole way. Write who carries what by hand on your printable evacuation plan, and repeat the test as the children grow.
actions.done: You have walked down your stairs and around the block with each carried child in a carrier and your packed bag worn on your front or carried by another adult, and who carries what is written on your evacuation plan.

actions.title: Leave a labeled overnight bag where your baby or toddler is cared for
actions.why: If roads or transit stop, the adults on the pick-up list may not arrive until morning, and a childcare's own stock will not match your child.
actions.how: Ask the childcare whether it will hold a bag for your child, and what its rules are for food and medicine. In it: four feeds of your child's formula (ready-to-feed where it is sold that way, otherwise unopened powder with sealed bottled water measured for each feed) or of the food your child eats, six diapers and wipes, a change of clothes, a comfort item, and a card with your numbers and the two other adults who may collect. Add a day's dose of any medicine only if the childcare agrees to hold it, with written instructions. Label the bag with the child's name and the date, and swap the contents every three months as sizes change and dates run out. The amounts are this site's suggestion; pack what your own child gets through in a night.
actions.done: The childcare has the bag, labeled with your child's name and today's date, and a reminder to swap its contents in three months is in your calendar.

actions.title: Arrange a safe sleep space for your baby at home and wherever you would go
actions.why: An emergency does not make an adult bed, a sofa, a carrier or loose bedding safe for a sleeping baby.
actions.how: Check that you have a crib, bassinet or portable play yard that meets current safety standards and fits your baby now, with the firm, flat mattress and fitted sheet made for it. Ask each place you would go (X2-03) whether it has one, and if not, decide who brings yours; a portable one also goes in the warm room at home on a cold night (FN-05). Every sleep is on the back, on that surface, with no pillows, loose blankets or soft toys and no adult sleeping bag; dress the baby for the room instead, with nothing covering the head. A baby who falls asleep in a carrier, car seat or stroller is moved onto the sleep surface as soon as you can. Write the arrangement by hand on your printable evacuation plan.
actions.done: The crib, bassinet or play yard your baby would sleep in is set up or packed, and your evacuation plan says what the baby sleeps in at each place you would go.

actions.title: Practice a way to feed your baby that needs no power
actions.why: A power outage, a broken pump or a parent's illness can interrupt feeding even when breast milk is the baby's usual food.
actions.how: Ask a lactation consultant, your midwife or your pediatrician's office to teach you hand expression before you need it; CDC notes that it takes no equipment, water or electricity. Keep clean collection cups and disposable feeding cups with the baby's supplies. If they advise cup feeding as your fallback, practice it with their guidance: the baby awake and held upright with head, neck and body supported, the rim of the cup at the lower lip, and the baby laps or sips. Never pour milk into the mouth. Decide who feeds the baby if the breastfeeding parent is away or ill, and what the baby would be fed (FN-01). If you store expressed milk, keep the freezer shut in an outage: milk that still has ice crystals can be refrozen, and milk that has thawed completely but still feels cold goes in the fridge, is used within a day or thrown away, and is never refrozen.
actions.done: The usual caregiver and one backup adult have each shown they can feed the baby by the agreed method, and both can point to where the cups are kept.

actions.title: Put an ID card in each child's bag and take a new photo every six months
actions.why: If you are separated, a card tells helpers who the child belongs to and a recent photo helps people find them.
actions.how: Print one blank wallet card per child and fill it in by hand: the child's full name, both parents' or carers' names and mobile numbers, your out-of-area contact, and any allergy or medical need a helper must know. Write the names the child uses, such as 'Grandma', beside the real names. Put the card inside the child's bag, not on the outside. Every six months take a new photo of each child, and one of you together, and keep them on your phone and printed in your own wallet.
actions.done: A filled-in wallet contact card is inside each child's bag, and a photo of each child from the last six months is on your phone and printed in your wallet.

actions.title: Get the pick-up and reunification plan from each school and childcare
actions.why: In an emergency you may not be the adult who reaches your child first, and a school will hand a child only to someone on its list.
actions.how: Ask each school, childcare, after-school program, club or camp five questions: where children are taken if the building is evacuated; how parents are told; who may collect a child and what ID they must show; how long staff stay with children whose parents are delayed; and, for a baby or toddler, what food, formula, diapers and medicine they hold if nobody can come until morning. Add two local adults besides you to each pick-up list, tell your child who they are, and check the list every September. Use a family password as one extra check, never as the only one; the school's own release rules decide who may collect a child, and a child who is unsure stays with staff. Write the answers by hand on each child's emergency numbers sheet.
actions.done: Each school and childcare has answered the five questions, two local adults are on each pick-up list, and the answers are written on each child's emergency numbers sheet.

actions.title: Teach children their address, your numbers and when to call 911
actions.why: A child who can say who they are, where they live and how to reach you gets back to you sooner.
actions.how: As soon as each child is old enough, teach them their full name, your full names, the home address and one parent's cell number, and repeat these aloud once a week until they stick. Practice a 911 call with the phone switched off: say your name, where you are and what is wrong, then stay on the line. Show them what the smoke alarm sounds like and where the paper contact list is kept. Tell children who have no phone to stay with a responsible adult such as their teacher.
actions.done: Each child old enough has said their full name, your names, the address and one cell number aloud, and has practiced a 911 call with the phone switched off.

actions.title: Pack comfort items for children
actions.why: A familiar toy, snack or game lowers a child's stress when everything else has changed.
actions.how: For each child, put a small familiar soft toy or blanket (a duplicate of the favorite if you can get one), a book, a pack of cards or a small game, and paper with pencils into the home kit. Add a few snacks they already like, and for a baby a spare of the pacifier or comforter they use now. Put a second, smaller set in the child's own bag. Let the child help choose, and swap items as they grow. By age, as this site's guide: under 2, a familiar blanket for when they are awake and two board books; ages 2 to 5, crayons, stickers, play dough and one new small toy held back for a bad day; ages 6 to 12, a chapter book, cards, a puzzle and a daily job; teenagers, their own charged power bank, headphones and a real role (FN-32). A baby under 1 sleeps with no blanket or soft toy in their sleep space (FN-34).
actions.done: Each child's comfort items are in the home kit, and a second, smaller set is in the child's own bag.

actions.title: Talk children through the plan
actions.why: Children cope better when they have been told in plain words what might happen and what the family will do.
actions.how: Pick a calm moment and use simple, matter-of-fact words: sometimes the lights, the heat or the phones stop working, and we have a plan for that. Show them where the lights and supplies are, walk the stairs together, and give each child one small job such as carrying their own headlamp. Let them ask questions, answer honestly for their age, and say it is fine to feel scared. Let them hear the smoke alarm test so the sound is familiar.
actions.done: Each child has been shown where the lights and supplies are, walked the stairs with you, been given one small job and heard the smoke alarm test.

actions.title: Match every child to a car seat and a driver
actions.why: A ride out is no use if your child cannot be buckled in safely.
actions.how: For each child, write down the seat they use now and its height and weight limits from the manual, which cars it fits, and which adults can install it. CDC's order is a rear-facing seat, then a forward-facing seat with a harness, then a booster until the seat belt fits, each used to the seat's own limit, with children in the back seat until age 13. Check there is a seating position for every person with the seats in place. For a relative's or neighbor's car, a taxi or a ride-hail, arrange the seat in advance: decide which seat goes with the child and show the named driver once how it fits. A baby carrier does not replace a car seat. In cold weather, take off a bulky coat or snowsuit before you buckle the harness, then lay a blanket, or the coat put on backward, over the buckled straps. Keep a way out on foot or by transit as the backup for a blocked road. A certified child passenger safety technician can check your installation; CDC's page links to a finder.
actions.done: Each child's seat, the cars it fits and the adults who can install it are written on your evacuation plan, and the named driver has fitted the seat once.

actions.title: Teach each child what to do if they lose you
actions.why: In a crowd, on stairs or at a shelter a child can be separated in seconds, and a child who stops is much easier to find than one who keeps walking.
actions.how: This is this site's suggestion, not an official rule. Teach one rule and practice it in a store: stop where you are and do not go looking; if nobody comes, ask a parent with children or a worker in uniform for help and show them your card (BG-20). Tell the child you will always come back to the last place you saw them. Before you go into any crowd, take a photo of each child on your phone as they are dressed that day, and write your cell number on a small child's forearm in pen.
actions.done: Each child has said the rule back to you and has practiced it once in a store.

actions.title: Give each child the part of the plan that fits their age
actions.why: A child with a job is calmer and more use than a child who is carried along, and what they can do changes every couple of years.
actions.how: These bands are this site's guide, not an official standard; go by what your own child can do. Under 3: no job; they stay with one named adult. Ages 3 to 5: knows their full name and a parent's first name, holds a hand on stairs, can point to the meeting place, carries their own small pack. Ages 6 to 9: knows the address and one cell number by heart, can call 911 and say where they are, knows the family password and two ways out of the home. Ages 10 to 13: can text the out-of-area contact, lead a younger child to the meeting place, use a headlamp and the radio, and knows not to open the door to strangers during an outage. Ages 14 to 17: carries an adult grab bag, knows where the shut-offs are, can mind a younger child for a short time, and holds their own contact card and transit fare. Review on each birthday.
actions.done: Each child has shown you their part once, for example said the address, pointed to the meeting place or sent a test text to the out-of-area contact.

actions.title: Write the one-adult version of leaving
actions.why: Most of the week one adult is at work, and the adult at home may have every child and every bag.
actions.how: On your printable evacuation plan, write by hand what changes when only one adult is home: which child is carried and which walks, which bag is left behind (take the documents, the medicines and the baby's feeds; leave the rest), and which neighbor on your floor has agreed to carry a child or a bag down the stairs. Ask that neighbor this week and offer the same in return. Set your reasons to leave (X2-05) earlier for this case, because you will move more slowly. Walk it once, alone with the children.
actions.done: The one-adult version is written on your evacuation plan, the named neighbor has said yes, and you have walked it once alone with the children.

actions.title: Write a medication list for each person
actions.why: With an accurate list, any doctor or pharmacist can replace your medicines even when the bottles and your records are out of reach.
actions.how: Print one blank medication list per person and fill it in by hand: each medicine's name, strength, dose and how often it is taken, what it is for, the prescriber and any allergies. Include inhalers, injections, eye drops, test strips, creams and regular over-the-counter medicines. Beside each prescription, write how often it is refilled, for example every 30 or 90 days. For 7 to 14 days, mark on paper every dose taken: who, which medicine and how many. Write each medicine's daily use on the list, multiply it by your target days (FN-12 shows the number, at least 7), and compare the result with what is at home. On the same list, write your pharmacy's name, address, phone number and hours, any after-hours number, your prescription or patient number if it uses one, and a second pharmacy you could walk to. Save both pharmacies' numbers in your phone. Keep one copy of the list in your document pouch and one in your wallet, and rewrite it whenever a medicine changes.
actions.done: Each person who takes regular medicine has a current handwritten medication list, with each medicine's daily use, how often it is refilled and two pharmacies on it, in the document pouch and in their wallet.

actions.title: Build a medication buffer with your prescriber's agreement
actions.why: Pharmacies can be shut or cut off from deliveries for days, and stopping some medicines suddenly is dangerous.
actions.how: Official guides suggest anything from 3 days to a month; this site aims for your target days with a minimum of 7, and shows the number from your household setup. Ask your prescriber and pharmacist three things: can I have an emergency supply or a 90-day prescription, how early can each refill be collected, and does my insurer allow an early refill? Keep only what they agree to, in the original labeled containers, refill on the first day allowed, and use the oldest first. If a disaster closes your pharmacy, the Rx Open online map shows which pharmacies in the affected area are open.
actions.done: Each prescriber has said how large an emergency supply you may keep and how early each refill can be collected.

actions.title: Plan how to keep refrigerated medicines cold
actions.why: Insulin and some other medicines lose strength when they get warm, and a refrigerator with no power stays cold for only about 4 hours with the door shut.
actions.how: Ask your pharmacist now, for each refrigerated medicine, how long it can stay out of the fridge and at what temperature, and write the answer on its box. Keep a small cooler, with ice packs or frozen water bottles in the freezer, ready to move the medicine into when the power fails or you have to leave. Wrap the ice packs in a cloth so the medicine does not touch them; insulin that has frozen must not be used. If a medicine has been warm for longer than its limit, call your pharmacist or doctor for a new supply, and if your life depends on it keep taking it until the new supply arrives.
actions.done: Each refrigerated medicine has its time-out-of-fridge limit written on the box and a cooler with frozen packs is ready.

actions.title: Ask your treatment provider for their emergency plan
actions.why: Dialysis, oxygen, infusions and home-care visits depend on clinics, deliveries and staff that an emergency can stop.
actions.how: Call each clinic, supplier or agency you rely on and ask: what happens if you lose power or I cannot reach you, which other site would treat me, who contacts whom, and how many days of supplies should I keep at home? Ask the equipment supplier for the model and serial number of each device and a 24-hour phone number. Write the answers by hand on the printable medical summary, and keep one copy by the door and one in your bag.
actions.done: Each clinic, supplier or home-care agency you rely on has told you its emergency plan and its answers are on the medical summary.

actions.title: Save the Poison Help number and lock up what you have stockpiled
actions.why: Getting ready puts more bleach, sanitizer, medicines and batteries in your home than before, and a child or a confused adult can get into them on an ordinary day.
actions.how: Save 1-800-222-1222 (Poison Help: free, 24 hours a day, anywhere in the United States) in every phone and write it on each emergency numbers sheet. Store the bleach, hand sanitizer, disinfectant, medicines (the spare supply and the bag's medicine pouch included) and spare batteries, button cells above all, in their original containers in a locked or latched cabinet, out of a child's sight and reach. Keep any bag that holds medicines zipped and off the floor. If someone swallows something they should not have, call Poison Help; call 911 if they are unconscious, not breathing or having a seizure.
actions.done: The Poison Help number is saved in every phone and written on each emergency numbers sheet, and the bleach, sanitizer, medicines and spare batteries are in a locked or latched cabinet.

actions.title: Fit safety latches or locks where medicines and cleaning products are kept
actions.why: Child-resistant caps slow a child down but are often not childproof, so the cabinet itself needs a latch or lock.
actions.how: Fit a safety latch or lock to every cabinet and drawer a child can reach that holds medicines, cleaners, laundry detergent, matches, lighters, or knives and other sharp things. Do it before your child starts to crawl or walk, or as soon as they do. Choose latches an adult can fit and open easily but that hold against a child's pulls and tugs, and pick the kind that locks by itself when the door shuts. Where a cabinet cannot take a latch, keep medicines in a locked box out of reach. FN-27 covers the Poison Help number and your stockpile.
actions.done: Every cabinet or drawer within a child's reach that holds medicines, cleaners, detergent, matches, lighters or knives has a latch or lock that stays shut when you tug the door.

actions.title: Keep cleaning products, laundry packets and other chemicals in their own containers, up and away
actions.why: The original container carries the directions, warnings and first-aid advice, and a chemical moved into a cup or drink bottle can be mistaken for a drink.
actions.how: Keep cleaners, bleach, pesticides and laundry packets in the containers they came in, and never pour them into a soda or juice bottle, a cup or a baby bottle. Close child-resistant caps tightly after every use, and close the product before you step away if you are interrupted. Store them out of children's sight and reach; a low cabinet needs a childproof latch or lock (FN-36). Do not let children handle laundry packets: they dissolve fast on wet hands or in the mouth, so handle them with dry hands and seal the tub and put it away after each load. If detergent from a packet gets in a child's eye, call Poison Help (FN-27) right away and rinse the eye with water for at least 15 minutes.
actions.done: Every cleaner, chemical and tub of laundry packets in the home is in its original labeled container, closed, in a latched cabinet or out of children's reach.

actions.title: Find every button and coin battery in the home and secure it
actions.why: A swallowed button or coin battery can burn through a child's throat in as little as two hours, and a used one can still do harm.
actions.how: Go room by room and find everything that runs on a small round battery: remotes, key fobs, thermometers, bathroom scales, watches, hearing aids, calculators, flameless candles, musical cards, toys and holiday decorations. Each battery compartment should need a screwdriver or coin to open; if it does not, or it is damaged, tape it shut and keep the item out of reach, or repair or get rid of it. Store spares as FN-27 says, check older children's things too, and hang keys up high. Cover a used battery in tape right away and take it to a battery collection point or put it in an outdoor trash can. Write the National Battery Ingestion Hotline, 800-498-8666, beside the Poison Help number. If you think a child has swallowed one, call 911 or go to an emergency department at once and say it may be a button battery. On the way, a child over 12 months who can swallow and swallowed it in the last 12 hours may be given 2 teaspoons (10 mL) of honey every 10 minutes, no more than 6 doses, only if you have honey on hand: give nothing else, do not make them sick, and never wait to find honey.
actions.done: Every device with a button or coin battery has a screwed or taped compartment or is out of reach, and the battery hotline number is written beside Poison Help.

actions.title: Put medicines away after every dose and keep visitors' bags out of reach
actions.why: About 100 young children a day are taken to an emergency room after getting into medicine left within their reach.
actions.how: Put every medicine, vitamin and supplement back in its high or latched place straight after each dose, even when the next dose is due in a few hours; do not leave it on the counter or at a sick child's bedside. Relock the cap every time: turn a twist-lock cap until it clicks or will not turn further. Ask babysitters, guests and visiting relatives to keep bags, purses and coats with medicine in them up high and out of sight, and give them a shelf or hook for it. Tell children what medicine is, that only a trusted adult gives it, and never call it candy.
actions.done: There is a high shelf or hook where visitors' bags go, and no medicine, vitamin or supplement is left out on a counter, table or bedside.

actions.title: Keep spare glasses, hearing-aid batteries and chargers in one place
actions.why: Losing the ability to see, hear or move around turns a manageable outage into a dangerous one.
actions.how: Put these into one labeled pouch beside the bed or in your bag: a spare or previous pair of glasses with a copy of the prescription, two unopened cards of hearing-aid batteries in the right size (or the charging case and cable), and the charger for any powered wheelchair or scooter. Add a spare cane tip, denture supplies and contact-lens solution if you use them. Note how long each mobility-aid battery lasts and how many hours it takes to charge, and add that to your power audit.
actions.done: Spare glasses, hearing-aid batteries or chargers and mobility-aid chargers are together in one labeled pouch.

actions.title: Wear or carry medical ID
actions.why: If you collapse or cannot speak, a bracelet or card tells a stranger in seconds what they must know.
actions.how: This is for anyone with a condition that changes emergency treatment, such as diabetes treated with insulin, epilepsy, a severe allergy, blood-thinning medicine, dementia or an implanted device. Get a bracelet or necklace engraved with the condition, the key medicine or allergy and one emergency phone number, or carry a card behind your photo ID. You choose what goes on it. Put a contact label on any wheelchair, walker or equipment bag as well. Wear or carry it every day, and fill in the emergency medical ID on your phone (MD-10) so that both say the same thing.
actions.done: Anyone whose condition changes emergency treatment wears or carries medical ID every day.

actions.title: Build a support network of three people
actions.why: Anyone who would need help to stay safe or to leave should not depend on a single person who may be away.
actions.how: If you or someone in your home would need help in an emergency, ask three people to be the network: one on your floor, one elsewhere nearby and one outside your area. Tell each what help is needed, where the supplies, medication list and care instructions are, and how any equipment works. Agree that they will check on you after an emergency without waiting to be asked, unless you have told them you are fine. Swap phone numbers and write theirs by hand on the emergency numbers sheet. Show them how to move you or your chair. Give one of them a spare key, and offer the same help in return.
actions.done: Three people have said yes, each has been told what help is needed and where things are kept, and their numbers are written on the emergency numbers sheet.

actions.title: Give a trusted neighbor a key
actions.why: If you are stuck across town or in the hospital, someone nearby can reach a relative, a pet or your medicines.
actions.how: Choose one person in your building or close by whom you trust and who is usually at home, and give them a spare key, plus a fob if your building uses one. Agree exactly when they may use it, for example when you ask, or when you cannot be reached for 24 hours in an emergency. Put no name or unit number on the key itself. Make sure the people in your support network know who holds it.
actions.done: The neighbor holds the spare key, and a fob if needed, has agreed when they may use it, and your support network has been told who holds it.

actions.title: Help relatives who live elsewhere make their own plan
actions.why: You may not be able to reach a parent across town or in another city during an emergency, so their plan has to work without you.
actions.how: Sit down together or call, and cover five things: emergency alerts switched on on their phone, a written medication list and a buffer of medicines, a week of water and food, a named neighbor who will check on them, and where they would go if they had to leave. Swap out-of-area contacts and agree how you will check in, including what happens if the phones are down, for example a visit after two days. Leave them their own paper copy.
actions.done: Each older or vulnerable relative who lives elsewhere has their own plan and kit.

actions.title: Write care instructions for anyone who depends on you
actions.why: If you are delayed or hurt, another adult must be able to take over the care of a child, a relative or a pet from a single page.
actions.how: Print the blank care instructions sheet, one per person or animal, and fill it in by hand. Cover the daily routine, food and anything they cannot eat, medicines with doses and times, how equipment works, how they communicate and what calms them, and the doctor's or vet's number. Give copies to your support network, and keep one by the door where a responder would see it and one in the bag. For a baby, write what to do when the crying will not stop: long spells of crying are normal for a baby, so check for signs of illness and call the doctor if you think the baby is sick; if you are getting upset, put the baby on their back in the crib, walk away to calm down and check on the baby every 5 to 10 minutes; call a friend, relative, neighbor or parent helpline for help; and never shake a baby. If you are the one who would need help, write a sheet about yourself too: the languages you speak, the conditions and allergies a helper must know about, and two people to notify. Keep each sheet to one page in plain words.
actions.done: Each person or animal who depends on you has a care-instructions sheet that a stranger could follow.

actions.title: Ask about paratransit and assisted evacuation
actions.why: Accessible transport often stops in an emergency, so a ride out has to be arranged before one is needed.
actions.how: If someone in your home uses paratransit or could not leave without help, call the provider and ask whether it runs during emergencies and evacuations and how to book. Call your city or county emergency management office and ask whether it keeps a register of people who need help to evacuate, and which shelters have step-free entrances and accessible bathrooms and accept service animals. Write the answers by hand on your printable evacuation plan. If an evacuation is ordered and you cannot get out, call 911 and give your address, floor and unit.
actions.done: Anyone who could not leave without help has asked about paratransit and assisted evacuation and written down the answers.

actions.title: Stock pet food, water and litter for your target days
actions.why: Pet stores and vets close in the same emergencies that close everything else, and your pet's usual food may not be on any shelf.
actions.how: The site works out food and water for your pets from your household setup. Water is planned at half a gallon per pet per day, which is this site's assumption, sized for a dog, and not an official figure; allow more for a large dog or hot weather. A cat needs much less: Cornell's veterinary college puts it at about 4 ounces a day for every 5 pounds of lean body weight, counting the water in its food. Ask your vet what your own animal needs. Food is each pet's normal daily amount for your target days. Buy the food your pet already eats, keep it sealed in a hard container, and use the oldest first. Add litter or pads for the same number of days, waste bags, and a reserve of any medicine, in the amount your vet agrees to. Keep a bowl and the water with the food so everything is in one place.
actions.done: The pet food and water the site works out are stored together with a bowl, waste bags and litter or pads, and the food is in a sealed hard container.

actions.title: Check you can get your pet down the stairs
actions.why: With the elevators out, a frightened animal has to go down the stairwell with you, in a carrier or on a leash you can hold.
actions.how: Do the stairs once with your pet. A cat or small animal goes in a secure carrier you can hold in one hand, so the other stays on the handrail; a dog goes on a fitted harness and a short leash. If a large dog cannot manage stairs, work out now who will help you carry it, and practice the lift with a blanket or sling. Leave the carrier out at home so your pet treats it as familiar, and keep it and the leash beside your bag.
actions.done: You have gone down the stairs once with your pet in its carrier or on its harness and leash, and both are kept beside your bag.

actions.title: Arrange a pet buddy who holds a key
actions.why: Emergencies often start while you are out, and someone nearby has to be able to reach your pet.
actions.how: Ask a neighbor who is usually at home, ideally one with pets, to be your pet buddy, and offer to be theirs. Fill in the printable pet sheet by hand, give your buddy a key, and show them where the sheet, carrier, leash and food are kept. Agree the rule: if there is an evacuation order or you cannot get home, they check on the pet and take it with them if they leave. Swap phone numbers and agree where you would meet afterward.
actions.done: Your pet buddy has said yes, holds a key and your number, and has been shown where the filled-in pet sheet, carrier, leash and food are kept.

actions.title: Plan for your pet in heat and cold
actions.why: Animals overheat and chill in the same conditions people do, and cannot tell you.
actions.how: In heat, keep your pet in the coolest room with you, with water always down and a damp towel or cool floor to lie on, and walk it only early or late. Heavy panting, drooling, weakness or vomiting in heat is an emergency: move the animal somewhere cooler and call a vet. In cold, keep walks short, dry your pet afterward, and put its bed off the floor and away from drafts. If your home is too hot or too cold for you to stay, it is not safe for your pet either, so take it with you.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the plan for heat and cold, and the pet's bed has a place off the floor and away from drafts.
actions.cite_todo: A veterinary source (AVMA) for the signs of heat stroke in pets and the first response.

actions.title: Keep a week of supplies where an older relative lives
actions.why: An older person living alone may be unable to carry water, wait in line at a store or get down the stairs for days.
actions.how: With your relative, set up at their home: 7 gallons of water in small bottles they can lift, a week of food they like that needs no cooking and that they can open, and their written medication list with the buffer their prescriber agrees to. Add a light beside the bed, a battery radio, a charged power bank, spare glasses and hearing-aid batteries, and key phone numbers in large print by the phone. Check dates and batteries at every visit, or at least twice a year.
actions.done: Your relative's home holds 7 gallons of water in bottles they can lift, a week of food they can open, their medication list, a bedside light and a radio.
